title: Geometric properties of sections
summary: This is the most computational subchapter in Chapter 1 and the most reliably scored, because almost every question reduces to one of five standard results plus the parallel axis theorem. Memorise the centroidal moments of inertia only — everything else follows from I = I_G + Ah². Two habits pay for themselves: check the power of length (I is mm⁴, Z is mm³, k is mm), and remember that moving material away from an axis increases I as the square of the distance, which explains the shape of every structural section.

sections.heading: Centroid and first moment of area
sections.body:
The centroid is the point through which the whole area could be concentrated without changing its **first moment** about any axis:

> **ȳ = Σ(A_i ȳ_i) / ΣA_i**

Composite sections are solved by taking moments of area about a convenient reference axis, with the areas of **holes or removed portions taken as negative**. That is the standard method for a channel, an unequal-flange I-section, or a circle with a segment cut away.

The shortcut that saves most of the work: **if a section has an axis of symmetry, the centroid lies on it.** A section with two axes of symmetry has its centroid at their intersection and needs no calculation at all.

**The standard centroids** — and note carefully which are **areas** (plane laminae) and which are **solids**, because the pairs are constantly confused:

| Shape | Centroid from the base / diameter |
|---|---|
| **Triangle** | **h/3** from the base |
| **Semicircular area** | **4r/3π** = 0.424 r |
| **Quarter circle** (area) | 4r/3π from **both** edges |
| **Semicircular arc** (a wire, not an area) | **2r/π** = 0.637 r |
| **Solid hemisphere** | **3r/8** = 0.375 r |
| **Solid cone** | **h/4** from the base |
| Solid pyramid | h/4 from the base |
| Rectangle | d/2 |
| **Trapezium** (parallel sides a, b; height h) | **h(2a + b)/(3(a + b))** from side b |

The traps in that table are worth stating explicitly. **3r/8 is the solid hemisphere**, not the semicircular area. And the **arc** differs enormously from the **area** (0.637 r against 0.424 r) because in the arc every element of length sits at the full radius, whereas in the area most of the material lies near the diameter where the shape is widest. The distinction between a **line, an area and a volume** is what the whole table turns on.

sections.heading: Moment of inertia and the two theorems
sections.body:
The **second moment of area** (loosely, moment of inertia) is **I = ∫y² dA**, in **mm⁴**.

**Parallel axis theorem:**

> **I_AB = I_G + A h²**

Because A is positive and h² can never be negative, the added term is **always ≥ 0**. Three consequences follow, and they are worth more than the formula:

1. I about any axis is **always greater** than about the parallel centroidal axis.
2. I is therefore **least about the centroidal axis** among all axes of that direction.
3. **Moving material away from the axis increases I as the square of the distance.**

That third point is the reason for the shape of nearly every structural section. An **I-section** places most of its material in the flanges, far from the neutral axis, making the Ah² term large; a solid rectangle of the same area wastes much of its material near the centre. It is also why a hollow tube is far stiffer than a solid rod of equal weight, and why the **depth** of a beam matters more than its width.

The theorem's essential condition: the axes must be **parallel** and one must pass through the **centroid**. Applying it between two arbitrary parallel axes, neither centroidal, is a standard error — go from the first to the centroidal axis, then out to the second.

**Perpendicular axis theorem** — for **plane laminae only**:

> **I_ZZ = I_XX + I_YY**

which gives the **polar** moment of inertia about an axis normal to the plane.

**The standard values.** Memorise only the centroidal column; the rest follow:

| Section | Centroidal | About the base |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle** b × d | **bd³/12** | **bd³/3** (× 4) |
| **Triangle** b × h | **bh³/36** | **bh³/12** (× 3), and **bh³/4** about the apex (× 9) |
| **Circle** d | **πd⁴/64** = πr⁴/4 | — |
| Semicircle r | 0.11 r⁴ | πr⁴/8 about the diameter |
| **Hollow circle** D, d | **π(D⁴ − d⁴)/64** | — |

Verifying the theorem once is worth memorising four formulae. Rectangle: bd³/12 + (bd)(d/2)² = **bd³/3** ✓. Triangle: bh³/36 + (½bh)(h/3)² = **bh³/12** ✓, and bh³/36 + (½bh)(2h/3)² = **bh³/4** ✓.

A hole is simply a **negative area**, provided both values are taken about the **same axis**. Where the removed portion is **not concentric**, apply the parallel axis theorem to it separately before subtracting.

sections.heading: Section modulus — strength
sections.body:
> **Z = I / y_max**,  in **mm³**

It comes straight from the flexure formula. Since **M/I = σ/y**, the stress is greatest at the extreme fibre:

> **σ_max = M / (I/y_max) = M / Z**,  so  **M = σ_max · Z**

So Z is the single geometric property that converts a bending moment directly into the maximum bending stress.

**Two properties answer two different questions**, and both must be checked:

| Property | Units | Governs | Question |
|---|---|---|---|
| **I** | mm⁴ | **Stiffness** — deflection | *How much will it deflect?* |
| **Z** | mm³ | **Strength** — bending stress | *Will it break?* |
| **k = √(I/A)** | mm | **Buckling** | *Will it buckle?* |

A deep, thin section can have a large I but, because y_max is also large, a proportionately smaller Z — so a section chosen for deflection is not automatically right for stress.

**Standard section moduli:**

| Section | Z |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** b × d | **bd²/6** |
| **Circle** d | **πd³/32** |
| Hollow circle | π(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32D) |

Note the **d²** in the rectangle. Doubling the **depth** multiplies moment capacity by **four**; doubling the **width** merely doubles it. That is why beams are deep rather than wide — and why laying a 50 × 200 mm joist flat instead of on edge reduces its capacity to a **quarter**.

**For an unsymmetrical section** — a T-beam, a channel — the distances to the top and bottom fibres differ, so there are **two** section moduli. The **smaller** governs where the material is equally strong in tension and compression; but for a material strong in compression and weak in tension (cast iron, concrete, masonry), the section is deliberately shaped so the **larger** y falls on the **compression** side.

**A dimensional habit worth forming.** Z has units of length³, so any option carrying d⁴ cannot be a section modulus whatever its coefficient. Checking the power of length first eliminates half the options in most questions of this family.

sections.heading: Radius of gyration and slenderness
sections.body:
> **k = √(I/A)**,  equivalently  **I = A k²**

It is the distance from the axis at which the whole area could be concentrated without changing I — a purely geometric measure of **how far the material is spread from the axis**. It is not a physical dimension of the section, and is always **less than the extreme fibre distance**.

**Standard values:**

| Section | k |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle** b × d, centroidal axis ∥ b | **d/√12** = 0.289 d |
| Rectangle, about the **base** | d/√3 = 0.577 d |
| **Circle** d | **d/4** |
| Hollow circle D, d | √(D² + d²)/4 |
| Square, side a | a/√12 |

Deriving the circle is pleasing and useful: k = √[(πd⁴/64)/(πd²/4)] = √(d²/16) = **d/4**. So the radius of gyration of a circle is a **quarter of its diameter**, and the slenderness ratio of a circular column is 4L/k... more precisely **L/k = 4L/d**.

Note that for the rectangle **b cancels** — k about that axis depends only on the depth.

**Where it is used: columns.**

> **slenderness ratio λ = L_eff / k_min**

and it is the **minimum** k that governs, because a column buckles about its **weakest** axis. For a rectangle that is the axis parallel to the **longer** side — so a 200 × 300 mm column buckles about the axis giving k = 200/√12, **not** 300/√12. Using the larger k overestimates capacity dangerously.

**Euler's formula** shows why it matters so much:

> **P_cr = π²EI/L_eff² = π²EA/λ²**

The critical load falls as the **square** of the slenderness ratio: a column twice as slender carries a **quarter** of the load.

Effective lengths: **both ends hinged L**, **both fixed L/2**, **one fixed one free 2L**, **one fixed one hinged L/√2**. So a fixed-fixed column carries **four times** the load of a pinned-pinned one of the same length.

**Why circular and square columns are efficient in compression:** their k is the same in every direction, so there is no weak axis to govern. A rectangle wastes material, because its strong axis can never be used to capacity.

sections.heading: Polar moment of inertia and torsion
sections.body:
By the perpendicular axis theorem, for a circle I_XX = I_YY = πd⁴/64, so

> **J = πd⁴/64 + πd⁴/64 = πd⁴/32**

The polar value is simply **twice** the diametral one — the fact worth carrying, since only one of the two need be remembered.

| Quantity | Circle of diameter d | Governs |
|---|---|---|
| **I** about a **diameter** | **πd⁴/64** | **Bending** |
| **J**, polar | **πd⁴/32** | **Torsion** |
| **Z**, section modulus | **πd³/32** | Bending **stress** |
| **Z_p**, polar modulus | **πd³/16** | Torsional **stress** |

**The torsion equation:**

> **T / J = τ / r = G θ / L**

giving the shear stress τ at radius r, and the angle of twist **θ = TL/GJ**. **GJ** is the **torsional rigidity**, exactly parallel to **EI** as the flexural rigidity.

**Why hollow shafts.** In torsion the shear stress varies **linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum at the surface**, so material at the core carries almost nothing. Removing the inner half of the diameter costs only **1/16** of the polar moment (since (½)⁴ = 1/16) while removing a quarter of the material. This is the same reasoning that puts the flanges of an I-beam far from the neutral axis: **material far from the axis of action does the work**.

**A worked comparison** for a solid 100 mm circle against a hollow one of 100 mm outside and 80 mm inside:

| | Solid | Hollow |
|---|---|---|
| Area | 7854 mm² | 2827 mm² — **36%** |
| I | 4.91 × 10⁶ mm⁴ | 2.90 × 10⁶ mm⁴ — **59%** |

The hollow section keeps **59% of the stiffness for 36% of the material** — a 64% improvement in stiffness per unit weight. That is the entire argument for tubes, pipes, hollow columns and box girders.

**Two cautions.** J = I_XX + I_YY holds only for a **plane lamina** about an axis perpendicular to its plane; and T/J = τ/r holds only for **circular** sections. Non-circular sections **warp** when twisted, and their torsional constant is not the polar moment of inertia at all.

**Why a circle is inefficient in bending but optimal in torsion.** Compared with a rectangle of equal area, a circle gives about **75% less** moment capacity, because it concentrates material near the neutral axis. In torsion the situation reverses: the shear is axisymmetric and no other shape avoids warping. Hence **circular sections for shafts, deep rectangular or I-sections for beams**.

sections.heading: Product of inertia and principal axes
sections.body:
> **I_xy = ∫ x y dA**

Unlike I_XX and I_YY, it can be **positive, negative or zero**, because x and y are **signed** coordinates.

**It vanishes when at least one axis is an axis of symmetry.** If the y-axis is symmetric, then for every element at (+x, y) there is an identical one at (−x, y); their contributions (+xy)dA and (−xy)dA **cancel exactly**, and integrating over the whole area gives zero.

Passing through the **centroid is not sufficient**. A **Z-section** or an **unequal angle** has centroidal axes about which I_xy is decidedly non-zero — which is precisely why those sections behave awkwardly.

**Principal axes** are those for which I_xy = 0, and about them I takes its **maximum and minimum** values:

> **tan 2θ = 2 I_xy / (I_yy − I_xx)**
> **I₁,₂ = (I_xx + I_yy)/2 ± √[((I_xx − I_yy)/2)² + I_xy²]**

The form is identical to the **principal stress** equations, and **Mohr's circle** may be drawn for moments of inertia exactly as for stress.

**Why an engineer must care.** Simple bending theory σ = My/I is valid only when bending occurs **about a principal axis**. Load an **unequal angle** in its geometric plane and it does not deflect in that plane at all: it deflects sideways and twists. This is **unsymmetrical bending**, and it is why:

| Situation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Angle sections used as **purlins** | Must be checked for unsymmetrical bending, or restrained |
| A column of **unequal angle** section | Buckles about a **principal** axis, not a geometric one |
| **Doubly symmetric** sections (I, box, circle) | Geometric axes **are** principal — the simple theory applies directly |

The last row is why standard rolled sections are doubly symmetric wherever possible: it keeps design simple and behaviour predictable.

**Two distinct minimisations**, easily conflated:

> Among axes of the **same direction** → the minimum is the **centroidal** axis (parallel axis theorem).
> Among **centroidal** axes of different **orientation** → the minimum is the **minor principal** axis.

A column-design question asks the second.

**And the sum is invariant.** For any pair of perpendicular axes through a given point, **I_xx + I_yy is constant** however the pair is rotated, since it equals the polar moment about that point. So rotating axes **trades** I_xx against I_yy without changing their sum — which is exactly why a section has both a maximum and a minimum principal value, ninety degrees apart.

**Shear centre**, closely related: the point through which a load must pass to cause **no twisting**. It coincides with the centroid for a **doubly symmetric** section, but for a **channel** it lies **outside** the section on the opposite side to the web — which is why a channel loaded at its centroid twists.

formulas.label: Centroid of a composite area
formulas.expression: ȳ = Σ(A_i ȳ_i) / ΣA_i    (holes taken as negative areas)
formulas.note: If the section has an axis of symmetry, the centroid lies on it — no calculation needed.

formulas.label: Parallel axis theorem
formulas.note: Ah² is never negative, so I is least about the centroidal axis. Both axes must be parallel and one centroidal.

formulas.label: Perpendicular axis theorem
formulas.note: Plane laminae only. Gives the polar moment of inertia about an axis normal to the plane.

formulas.label: Section modulus
formulas.expression: Z = I / y_max    (mm³);   σ_max = M / Z
formulas.note: Rectangle bd²/6, circle πd³/32. Two values for an unsymmetrical section.

formulas.label: Radius of gyration and slenderness
formulas.expression: k = √(I/A);   λ = L_eff / k_min;   P_cr = π²EI/L_eff²
formulas.note: A column buckles about its minimum k. Critical load falls as the square of slenderness.

formulas.label: Polar moment of inertia and torsion
formulas.expression: J = πd⁴/32 (solid circle);   T/J = τ/r = Gθ/L
formulas.note: J is twice the diametral I. Hollow: J = π(D⁴ − d⁴)/32. Circular sections only.

formulas.label: Principal axes
formulas.note: I_xy = 0 when an axis is an axis of symmetry. I_xx + I_yy is invariant under rotation.
